title: Building a free social MMO life sim in the browser as a tiny team: what worked, what didn't (open alpha)
md:
*Disclosure: I'm building Towneers, the game I'm writing about. This is a founder's notebook from an open alpha, not a success story. I'm not sharing player or revenue numbers because we don't publish them, and I'd rather leave a gap than make one up.*

## What we're building

Towneers is a free multiplayer pixel-art life simulation that runs in the browser, on a phone or a computer, with nothing to download. Everyone shares one always-on isometric city. You get a job, open a café or a shop, rent or buy a home, build a house on your own plot, farm, craft, fish, ride a scooter or drive a car, and meet real people along the way. Named characters are real players. Over 750 computer-controlled residents fill the streets between them.

A few facts from the game's own data, so you can judge the scope: 297 buildings, 91 land plots, 443 items, 198 crafting recipes, 24 kinds of workstations, 19 jobs and professions, and 28 kinds of place a player can open. It speaks five languages: English (the default), Spanish, German, Ukrainian and Russian. It is in alpha: balance changes, bugs happen, and the world may be reset. That last part matters for everything below, because it shapes how honest we have to be.

## Why this product

I'll start with what I did not want to build. I did not want a game where every task is a chore you do alone and the other players are decoration. A shared city with a chat window is not a social game. Plenty of multiplayer products are single-player experiences with other people's avatars walking past.

The bet behind Towneers is narrower and more specific: **a social economy**. If people need each other to get the best deals, they talk. If a café owner can post "we buy perch for this price, up to this many a day", a fisher has a reason to walk in and say hello. If a team can rent a factory hall and split the payout between those who put in money and those who put in work, a group of friends has something to run together.

So we wrote down one rule for the economy and have kept returning to it: the computer-controlled city should never be more profitable than a human. The city buys at a floor price, below what players usually pay each other. It keeps the basics running, and it is deliberately a worse customer than a person. The best prices, the best quality and the best stories are meant to come from people.

Does it work? In a small alpha, I can describe the mechanics with certainty and the human outcome with caution. The mechanics are real and checkable. Whether they reliably make strangers friends is exactly the kind of question an alpha is for.



Two reasons, one practical and one strategic.





## The tech choices that keep costs low

I'll keep this section short, because the technical details deserve their own articles (I wrote a few). What matters for a founder is the cost shape.

- **One server process.** The backend is plain Node.js with an authoritative server that owns the world. It has exactly one runtime dependency: `ws`, for WebSockets. No framework, no ORM, no bundler on the client.
- **Data in files.** The world lives in memory and is saved to JSON files on disk, written atomically (temp file, then rename). The storage interface was designed so that it can be swapped for a real database later without touching game logic. It is honest about its limits: everything must fit in memory and it does not scale across machines. For one game on one server, the simplicity is worth more than the headroom.
- **Shared code.** The same ES modules run on the server and in the browser: item and recipe registries, the economy table, price rules, even deterministic city generation. A number that appears on a player's screen and the number the server settles are produced by the same function. That removes a whole category of "the UI said X but I got Y" bugs and support tickets.
- **A custom canvas renderer.** No game engine. Heavy sprite work happens in a background worker, so the frame doesn't freeze while the city draws.
- **One VPS.** According to our deployment notes, a small virtual machine runs a stage and a prod instance behind nginx and Cloudflare. I'd double-check the exact specs before quoting them as current, but the shape is the point: there is no cluster, no managed database and no queue service to pay for or babysit.
- **Content as data.** Game processes are described as scenarios, JSON graphs that the game itself reads for loot tables, hints and the in-game guide. Tuning values are editable from an admin panel without a release.

What this buys is a short list of things that can break, a bill I can explain in one sentence, and the ability for a tiny team to hold the whole system in their heads. What it costs is that we write things ourselves that a library would give for free, and that a bigger audience will force some of these decisions to change. I'd rather pay that cost when it's real than before.





## Monetization: optional, and from $1

Towneers is free to play with no time limits. The optional purchases are gems 💎 and Premium, starting from $1. Premium for 30 days costs $4.99, and every price in the shop is in US dollars on the public shop page.

The reasoning, in order of importance:

1. **The world is the product, and an empty world is worthless.** Paywalling the core loop would shrink the population and the economy that makes the game interesting. The game is free, and gold is earned in play.
2. **Cosmetic and convenience purchases fit a social world.** People like to look different and to have a bit more room or time. Some vehicles are exclusive to gems, while seven cars are bought with in-game gold.
3. **Low entry price.** A $1 starting point is a deliberate choice for a product in alpha, where trust is the scarce resource and nobody should feel they bought into something they can't yet judge.

I won't claim this model is proven, and I won't share conversion numbers, because we don't publish them. What I can say is that the alpha label is also a promise: we state clearly that the world may be reset and balance may change. If you're building something similar, I'd suggest putting that on the page where people pay, not only in a FAQ.

## Growth: the channels we're testing

We're a small team, so we picked channels that compound and don't require a paid-acquisition budget to learn from. None of these has a result I'm ready to brag about, so read this as a list of experiments.

### 1. Content and SEO

A browser game has an odd SEO problem: the product is a canvas and a WebSocket, which a crawler sees as an empty page. The words that can rank, and that an assistant can quote, have to live elsewhere. So we built:

- a server-rendered **blog** and a **game guide** (the same engine, no client JavaScript), in five languages, with hreflang only for languages that really exist, real canonical URLs and a policy that untranslated pages don't compete with themselves;
- **guides that answer a real question**: how to open a café, how to get a house, how to earn on a farm, how fishing works, how to run a factory with friends, and how to earn your first 1,000 gold. Every number in the evergreen guide pages comes from the game's live data through a placeholder, so a page can't drift away from the economy after a balance change;
- **structured data** (`BlogPosting`, `FAQPage`, `HowTo`, and the game itself described as a `VideoGame`) and Open Graph images, because link previews matter more to a social game than any search engine.



### 2. Long guides as the main bet

Our best guess is that **depth beats volume**. A thin post about "5 tips" competes with thousands of near-identical posts. A deep farming guide with every crop, every seed tier, the plot prices and a daily plan is something few people will bother to write, because it requires access to the real game data. That is the one advantage a small studio has over a content farm. We have long guides for farming, fishing, teams and factories, and for owning a plot and a house.

### 3. Written for machines, too

We also publish `llms.txt`, a full-text file, and a markdown version of every page at the same address plus `.md`. I don't claim this moves rankings: I don't know of public evidence that the major search engines use `llms.txt` as a ranking signal, and a lot of what's said about it online is speculation. We keep it because it costs almost nothing, it reuses data we already have, and some assistants and developer tools do fetch it. Our robots file also welcomes AI crawlers on the blog and guide, and disallows the game itself, since there's nothing to index in a canvas. For a free game that lives on recommendations, an assistant suggesting it is distribution, so we made that decision on purpose and wrote the reasoning into the file.





### 4. Referral links with per-channel tracking

Every channel we use gets its own short link of the form `/r/<channel>`. The server records the click and redirects to the landing page or into the game. Links from articles into the game use UTM parameters, with the article slug as the campaign. The point is simple: **if a channel doesn't have its own link, we can't learn from it**. We also decided that nothing gets posted to a community without a human reading and approving it first. That slows us down. It also keeps us out of the "obvious promotion" trap that burns founders in exactly the communities they most want to be part of.

## Measurement: what we look at

I want to be specific about the instruments, and honest that measuring a small product is mostly about not fooling yourself.

- **Search Console** for what people searched when they found us, which pages are indexed and which are not, and whether our hreflang setup is being read correctly.
- **IndexNow.** On production, a small job reads our own sitemaps every thirty minutes and pushes new and changed URLs to the search engines that support the protocol, instead of waiting for them to poll. It records what it sent, so a failed push is retried. Google doesn't support IndexNow, so for Google the sitemaps remain the way in.
- **Per-channel links and UTM tags,** so a visit can be traced to a channel, a catalog or an article.
- **AI-visibility checks.** We periodically ask assistants the questions our guides answer, and look at whether the game is mentioned and whether the facts are right. This is manual and imprecise, and I treat it as a smell test, not a metric. It's also a way to find wrong facts about your own product, which is useful on its own.
- **Server-side logs by user agent,** because UTM tags only survive when an assistant keeps them.
- **The onboarding funnel,** a step-by-step view of where new players drop out during the tutorial. For a social game, the first minutes decide whether anyone ever sees the part that makes it interesting.

What I'm deliberately not doing is publishing a dashboard of vanity numbers. They'd be small, noisy and misleading at this stage.

## What worked, what didn't (so far)

**What I'd repeat**

- **Writing rules down as data.** Scenarios, registries and tuning tables mean we can change the economy from an admin panel and have the site, the guide and the in-game cards stay in agreement. It also makes a tiny team feel bigger.
- **One mechanic, one place.** Crafting goes through one window, buying through one cart, trading through one market. Early on we let several versions of the same thing appear, and we paid for it in confusion and bugs. We stopped.
- **Making the economy hard to fake.** The market price shown on an item card is a median of real deals between real people, and it only appears when there are enough deals between enough different players. Deals between accounts that look like the same person, or that repeat between the same pair, or that sit far outside the median, don't count. It's the kind of invisible work no player will thank us for, and it's what makes the number trustworthy.


**What didn't work, or isn't proven**

- **Doing everything at once.** The game has a large surface: housing, farms, factories, vehicles, a funfair and leaderboards. Breadth makes the first impression harder to control, and I suspect we sometimes pay for it in new-player focus.
- **Treating content as a quick win.** Content compounds slowly, and an honest answer to "is the SEO working?" at this stage is "too early to say." Anyone selling you a faster story is guessing.



## Open questions

These are the real ones, the ones I'd love to hear other founders' views on.

1. **Does a social economy create friendships, or just trades?** We designed incentives for talking to strangers. I'd like to know how to tell the difference between two people who trade and two people who play together.
2. **How early do you show a price?** A market index needs deals before it's honest, and a new market has few deals. We fall back to a static reference until there's enough data. Is that the right trade-off?
3. **Where does a free social game's money come from without turning pushy?** Optional purchases from $1 and a 30-day Premium at $4.99 are our current answer. I'm not convinced it's the final one.
4. **Do long guides keep working as assistants answer more questions directly?** If a model summarises our farming guide, does the reader ever visit? We'd rather be the cited source than the ignored one, but I don't know yet whether that converts.


## If you want to look

If you're curious how any of this feels in practice, the game is free and opens in any browser. Pick a character, walk into the city, and see whether it does what I've described. If something doesn't match my description, I want to know. [towneers.world](https://towneers.world/r/devto?utm_campaign=founder-story&utm_content=article)

The guides, the blog and `llms.txt` live at [towneers.world](https://towneers.world). And if you've built a persistent shared world as a small team, I'd especially like to hear what you wish you'd measured earlier.
